literary_identity: Labouring-class or peasant poet, hedge-layer and day-labourer in husbandry, topographical and bird poet, and a systematic natural historian of one fen-edge parish; the central figure of English rural labouring poetry after Bloomfield.
biography: John Clare was born on 13 July 1793 in West Street, Helpston, then in Northamptonshire and afterwards in the Soke of Peterborough, the eldest son of Parker Clare, a farm servant whose wages fell until he lived on parish relief, and of Ann Parker. He had little formal schooling, taught himself from a handful of borrowed books, and began verses in his teens. He worked as a shepherd boy and then as a hedge-paler and day-labourer, and the enclosure of the Helpston commons and sheep-walks in 1809 gave his earliest mature poems their subject of dispossession. In 1819 he put out a manuscript volume entitled The Shepherd's Calendar; it reached local patrons, came to the notice of the Rev. Brownlow North, Lord Radstock, and through the Stamford bookseller Edward Drury reached John Taylor of Fleet Street, who with Radstock organised the subscription. Poems Descriptive of Rural Life and Scenery, carrying on its title page the designation the Northamptonshire Peasant, was published in March 1820 for Taylor and Hessey and sold some four thousand copies within weeks, making Clare a metropolitan celebrity; Taylor took him to London, the subscribers' surplus provided him with a cottage at Helpston, and he married Patty Turner in August 1820, fathering a large family. The Village Minstrel and Other Poems followed in 1821 and sold far less well; The Shepherd's Calendar with Village Stories appeared in 1827 through John Taylor, and The Rural Muse in 1835 by subscription, both poorly received. Signs of mental illness appeared in the early 1830s, and in July 1837 Clare was admitted to the private asylum at High Beach in Epping Forest kept by Dr Matthew Allen, passing in 1841 into the same physician's Northamptonshire practice at Castle Eden and Highbeecote, where he remained above twenty years, was visited by Wordsworth in 1841, and was allowed regular returns to Helpston. In 1863 he was moved to the county institution, the Northampton General Lunatic Asylum, where he died on 20 May 1864 and was buried on 25 May in the churchyard at Helpston. Manuscript poetry of the confinement years, including the bird pieces, the autobiographical The Misanthropos, and the lyric I Am, was recovered only in the twentieth century.
literary_profile: His printed canon is small and heavily mediated by publishers, while the manuscript canon is enormous: memorandum volumes of the Helpston and confinement years, bird-nest registers, and records of weather, plants, and birds, alongside thousands of sonnets. The fourteen-line sonnet he developed on his own, without an accepted pattern, carries much of his best work. His poetry is at once topographical, encyclopaedic, and elegiac, holding precise field observation and the complaint against enclosure in a single line of thought, and his late lyrics on identity, memory, and derangement are the strongest part of his modern reputation.
stylistic_characteristics: A close ear for the speech of the Northamptonshire and Soke fen-edge and for the names of birds, plants, and field tasks; a syntax that runs in parataxis after the sense rather than after grammatical rule; heavy use of the present participle and of demonstrative deictics; a rhyming ear that prefers the exact and homely word; and a fourteen-line sonnet in which octave and sestet turn on a single perceived image rather than on argument.
intellectual_concerns: Enclosure and the loss of common ground; the relation of local knowledge to printed authority; the rights of the labourer to leisure and to authorship; the observation of nature as a form of piety; selfhood, memory, and derangement; the tyranny of grammar, spelling, and editorial correction over a dialect voice; fame, patronage, and dependence.
historical_significance: He is the culminating figure of the eighteenth-century labouring-class poetic tradition and, in critical estimation from the 1960s onward, a major Romantic poet rather than a curiosity. His vogue of 1820 shows the mechanism of Romantic patronage and subscription at work on a peasant hand, and his printed text shows what that mechanism cost a dialect writer in revision. His posthumous manuscripts made him a central authority for twentieth-century nature writing and for the cultural history of the enclosure of the English commons.
major_influences: James Thomson's The Seasons
Bloomfield's The Farmer's Boy
the eighteenth-century sonnet writers
Wordsworth and the reviews of the Lyrical Ballads
the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer
Scott's poetry
the Helpston oral tradition of bird and field naming
his own reading in subscription libraries and parish books.
biographical_uncertainty: The printed texts of 1820 to 1835 were altered by John Taylor, by the patronal circle, and later by Robert Chambers, so the degree to which the published dialect represents Clare's practice is unsettled. His diagnosis has been argued variously as manic depression, epilepsy, porphyria, and the effects of alcohol, without consensus. Dates of many confinement poems rest on manuscript rather than documentary evidence, and the account of his second partnership at Helpston and of the burial of his heart there rests on family tradition. Two particulars are often mis-stated in secondary accounts: his birthplace is Helpston, though the poem and the early title pages print Helpstone, and his 1837 admission was to a private house in Essex, the Northampton county asylum following only in 1863; he died at Northampton and was buried at Helpston.

literary_identity: Journeyman shoemaker and rural poet, the first labouring-class writer in England to reach a mass reading public, and the author of the seasonal countryside poem that created the market into which Clare and the mechanic poets of the 1810s were afterwards launched.
biography: Robert Bloomfield was born on 3 December 1766 at Honington in Suffolk, the son of George Bloomfield, a tailor whose trade failed, and of Elizabeth Bloomfield, a village schoolteacher who gave him his earliest lessons. Removed from school to work while still a boy, he earned his living in country service and then in London as a journeyman shoemaker, working at his trade among Cheap-side houses, and he composed verse in garret lodgings after hours of hand labour, describing the poet's whole domain of that period as a garret. The Farmer's Boy, a rural poem in four parts following the working year of a farm household from spring ploughing to the winter fire-side, was published in 1800, printed for Vernor and Hood of London, and its success was immediate and sustained: it ran through many editions and reached a cumulative circulation put at some twenty-five thousand copies, the largest for a single poem of the labouring-class tradition. The book made him the most famous working man of letters of his generation and drew patrons about him, among them the Duke of Grafton, whose support included a small annuity, and it established the model of the discovered and edited peasant poet on which every later case was formed. Prosperity was repeatedly undone by the size of his family, by the hard terms on which his copyright and his labour were bought, and by the poor sale of his later books, which returned to the same seasonal and domestic material in ballad and easy descriptive measure. His last years were spent in Bedfordshire, where he lived in reduced circumstances at Shefford, and he died there on 19 August 1823, being buried in the churchyard at Campton near Shefford, where his grave has been the site of commemorations by the society that bears his name. His correspondence, which records the working of subscription, patronage, and provincial bookselling around a journeyman hand, survives in modern scholarly edition, and his family papers and letters are the chief evidence for the circle of labouring writers that gathered about him.
literary_profile: His career is almost identical with one book. The Farmer's Boy adapts the Thomsonian seasonal estate poem to the working calendar of an East Anglian and Midland household, keeping the closed couplet of the eighteenth-century didactic manner but filling it with the tool, animal, sound, and task vocabulary of actual husbandry; the accompanying poems, tales, and lyric numbers rework the same material in the popular stanzas of the period. The volume that carried his name was framed by prefixed matter and by illustrations, making him an early instance of a labouring poet whose text was shaped as a commodity for a genteel subscribing market.
stylistic_characteristics: Closed iambic heroic couplets of the plain rural school, with a low and concrete vocabulary of field tasks, weather, animals, and domestic economy; frequent apostrophe to personified abstractions held decorously; a strong sense of the working day rather than of incident; provincial Suffolk and Bedfordshire household speech; and a sentimentality of pathos carried by detail rather than by rhetoric.
intellectual_concerns: The dignity and the exhaustion of regular labour; the rural year as an ordered world; depopulation, low wages, and the distress of the labouring parish in the dear years of the 1790s; patronage, copyright, and the economics of authorship for a working man; temperance, dependence, and self-respect; the education of a reader's eye through the seasons.
historical_significance: He created the reading market that afterwards received the mechanic and peasant poets of the 1810s and 1820s, and he established the labouring-class countryside poem as a publishable form. His career documents both the possibility and the limits of patronage and subscription for working-class authors, and the garret-to-popularity plot he supplied was repeated and resisted by later labouring poets, Clare chief among them, whose first volume was built on the model his sales had made fashionable.
major_influences: James Thomson's The Seasons
the eighteenth-century topographical and estate poem
Goldsmith's The Deserted Village and the depopulation lament
Cowper's domestic descriptive manner
the Bible and the hymn-book
and the popular pastoral of his own reading in Suffolk.
biographical_uncertainty: The cumulative sales of The Farmer's Boy and the size of its earliest print runs vary between accounts, and the twenty-five thousand figure is an approximation from bibliographical rather than from trade records. The publisher of the first edition is recorded in bookseller descriptions as Vernor and Hood, while later editions passed through other hands. Three particulars long attached to his career were not confirmed from primary titles during this review and should be checked against the copies themselves: the hand-coloured plate editions associated with Rudolph Ackermann and with the drawings of William Henry Pyne, a medal or premium from the Society of Arts, and a burial grant or permission connected with Westminster Abbey. The attribution of the prefixed account of the author to John Aikin, and the dating and imprint of a two-volume collection of 1813, are likewise matters on which secondary accounts disagree.

literary_identity: Comic verse-maker, essayist, and magazine and annual editor of the London periodical trade, with an unsuccessful ambition to be a serious poet; the founding figure of the English punning comic verse tradition and one of the most reprinted poets of the mid-Victorian anthologies.
biography: Thomas Hood was born on 23 May 1799 in London, in the Poultry in Cheapside, the son of a bookseller and publisher of Scottish Presbyterian origin whose death in 1811 left the family in straits. Withdrawn from school for a merchant's counting house and then bound to learn engraving in his maternal uncle's London workshop, he ran away northward as an apprentice and passed some years in Scotland, working as a journalist and schoolmaster before returning to London. From 1821 he was attached to the London Magazine as sub-editor and contributor after the death of its first editor, and for the next twenty-four years he was engaged, as writer or editor, with most of the leading London periodicals, among them the Athenaeum, the New Monthly, and the keepsake annuals. In 1825 he married Caroline Reynolds, sister of the poet John Hamilton Reynolds, with whom he had already collaborated in burlesque verse, and the burden of a growing household and of chronic ill health fixed his subsequent career in the market. Whims and Oddities, first series, appeared in 1826 and the second series in 1827, the two volumes making his name with the public; National Tales, two volumes of novella imitation, and The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies, his one book of serious verse, followed in 1827. He edited the annual The Gem from 1829, giving early pages to Tennyson, and founded and conducted The Comic Annual from 1830 into the 1840s, while his ballad of the murderer's dream was reprinted separately in 1831 from the annual pages. Speculative ventures in publishing and on the stage, a novel of 1834, and a long residence abroad for his health, recorded in a travel book of 1840, left him in debt and in permanent overwork, and he wrote for the magazines and for Punch into the last years of his life. He died at his home at Finchley Road, London, on 3 May 1845, was buried on 10 May at Kensal Green cemetery, and was memorialised there in 1854 by a monument paid for by public subscription, an unusual testament to a writer of comic verse.
literary_profile: His work divides between a serious poetry of fairy legend, melancholy ballad, and seasonal meditation, represented by The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies, Hero and Leander, and the ballad-poem on Eugene Aram, and an enormous comic output of punning song, parody, and sketch in prose and verse. He also wrote prose tales, a novel, editorial and reviewing matter for magazines and annuals, and the account of his continental exile. The social lyrics of his last years, on the seamstress, the lost child, and the bridge of sighs, converted his command of the popular stave into the most quoted humanitarian verse of the 1840s and held his place in the school anthology for a century.
stylistic_characteristics: In the comedy, an accumulating engine of homonym, internal rhyme, refrain, and mock-earnest rhetoric driven to the point of collapse, with the argument of a sketch abandoned to the pursuit of the joke. In the serious and sentimental verse, a measured descriptive line of the eighteenth-century school above a ballad stave, with a fondness for the dying child, the drowned bride, and the vanished fairy. The two manners coexist in the same volumes, and the pun survives even into the elegy.
intellectual_concerns: The psychology of guilt and of concealed crime; the decay of popular fairy belief under tillage and improvement; the poverty, debt, and dependence of the professional hack; the relation of comic verbal play to genuine feeling; the labour and distress of paid workers in a factory town; the uses and the failures of the annual and the periodical as a literary economy.
historical_significance: He is the source of the nineteenth century's punning comic verse tradition, inherited by the joke-book, the music hall song, and the magazine wit, and one of the most reprinted poets of the mid-Victorian period. His double career measures the gap between Romantic ambition and its commercial reward, and his editorial work in the annual and the comic keepsake is a document of the gift-book economy at its height, while the later labour lyrics supplied a lasting model for verse on industrial poverty.
major_influences: John Hamilton Reynolds and the Hunt circle
Charles Lamb and the familiar essay
the burlesque and jest-book tradition of Peter Pindar and opera parody
Thomson's descriptive manner
the lyrical ballad as he read it in the magazines
and the popular song stave of London performance.
biographical_uncertainty: His birth year is occasionally given as 1798 in older reference works, but 23 May 1799 is the received entry date. The year in which he took up work at the London Magazine, whether early or late in 1821, and the exact share of his editorial responsibility are variously reported. The publisher of the first series of Whims and Oddities is given differently in modern bibliographies, and the imprint requires checking against the copy; his contributions to Blackwood's Magazine, often asserted, were not confirmed during this review. The standard Victorian memoir written by his daughter compresses the chronology of his debts and of his Scottish years.
